verdict.reasoning: Reproduced in the engine and on the page. In carriedHit (engine.js:2686-2688) the reported carry.F is cf.soft.F, the force that alone gives Rex pGain over T, so F*T = pGain exactly. But supplied = pGain + footJ. The force between the two bodies, whose push back goes to Ollie's source, must therefore average (pGain + footJ)/T = F + footF. So the 'Force of the hit' tile, the 'Forces at the hit' bar and the squash paragraph understate the hit by the hold in every carried splat. Nothing on the page or in the README discloses this. It is 7% at the page default, 1% all-out, 44% unflagged for a bolted Rex on real rock, and 2.2x for a jump onto Rex on real ground. The min(Hhold, F) cap is a stated decision (decision 1, Known limit 3), and the page does say 'rough' where it bites, including at 1 m/s on friction, a case the README limit doesn't name. But its reason, 'the push rises until it gives', does not hold in the lab's own constant-force squash. Taking the engine's splatWithFooting (engine.js:2307) with mA -> infinity gives F' = mB v^2/(2s) + H, the same tau, and Jearth = H*tau with no cap, from the start of the hit. That matches the engine exactly where F > H. Where F < H the cap undercounts the ground's share: 3,000 vs 11,100 kg m/s at 1 m/s, 49,700 vs 57,700 for the jump. Test 8a's footWant = min(H, F)*T builds the cap into the test. One small slip in the finding's own evidence: (255 - 17.7) kN x 0.086 s = 20,400 kg m/s is 6.80 m/s, not 6.98. The conclusion stands.

verdict.reasoning: Reproduced. armWrestle (engine.js:1819) checks only the winner's pad. With the winner's power on, that pad is set to the loser's press Pl, and the page, the README and test 8i conclude that a pin never breaks the table. The engine's own rigid-forearm mechanics also load the loser's pad. They are the same mechanics behind the power-off formula R_w = C + holdArm*mw*a, with C = Pl + effMass*ml*a. The loser's forearm turns about his elbow, and its centre of mass needs m_fl*a_cm = holdArm*ml*a. The hand contact C supplies only part of that, so his elbow pivot, held by his pad, carries |holdArm*ml*a - C|. That force acts on the loser, not on the winner. It isn't the winner's push back, and it isn't a push the loser makes on anyone, so neither one's own-recoil absorption removes it. With the power off this load never mattered, because for equal masses the winner's pad load is always larger. With the power on, the winner's pad drops to Pl and the loser's pad becomes the larger load. In the README's own example it is 24.2 kN against a 15.1 kN table, 1.6x, so the table breaks in the pin and the standing contest follows. Under reading B taken literally (the loser's pad holds the winner's press less what spins his forearm) it is 85.8 kN, 5.7x. In test 8i's own grid, 420 of the 2,160 runs pin on the table while the loser's pad, by the engine's model, is past the table's limit. The test can't see them because it never computes that load. This only affects Things keep their form off with unequal strengths, but the claim is stated as a rule on the page, in decision 10 and in the 'What moved' bullet.

findings.title: Arm wrestling, decision 10: the case against the brief's reading A is wrong, and B absorbs nothing in a stalemate
findings.location: rex-strength-lab/README.md:168 (decision 10); rex-strength-lab/src/engine.js armWrestle comment (lines ~1773-1790) and the stalemate path
findings.evidence: README: 'Under A ... With nothing on his side carrying it, a real force would act on each hand in a stalemate while nothing moved: momentum would vanish outside canon's list.' In arm wrestling the two presses meet at one contact, the clasped hands. 'The other's press on him' and 'the push back of his own press' are therefore the same contact force C. What each puts on himself is his own arm's reaction at his elbow and shoulder, which under the rules lands on the pad. Under A that reaction goes to his source (canon's case 'their own recoil'). Each hand is held by his own arm, whose push is real, so nothing moves, and the shared source receives −C·t and +C·t: nothing vanishes outside the list. Under B the pad keeps that reaction. In a stalemate nothing is absorbed, exactly as with the power off. Engine at the default dial with Things keep their form off: armWrestle gives tableBreaks true, tableBreaksBy 'push' at 222 kN with ownRecoil true, and the same with it off; no recoilAbsorbed in a stalemate. Q12 says 'The only absorption is the push each puts on himself'. The results differ: B breaks the table (courtesy ceiling 6.7%, 6.1 t, 'the table tears apart') and then reports both pushed off their feet standing. Under A the author's own count is 0 of 2,160 runs breaking the table.
findings.expected: A decision that departs from the brief's reading needs a sound reason. A is physically coherent and matches Q12's wording. B keeps the old physics for every stalemate.
findings.fix: Either build reading A, where with the power on the presses don't load the pads and the table carries only the slam, or keep B. If B stays, correct decision 10 (README and engine comment) to say that A is coherent and B is a choice, and ask the owner to choose with the concrete differences (the table break at 6.1 t, the standing 'both pushed off their feet').

verdict.reasoning: Not a defect. Decision 10 is a recorded choice with a sound reason, and it is flagged to the owner in 'What is left' ('arm-wrestling reading B (decision 10)'). The duo's version of A works by letting each one's source take his own arm's reaction at the elbow and shoulder. In a stalemate that reaction equals the other's press, so his source in effect holds him against the other's real press. That is Never knocked back, which canon sets aside in contests ('In a contest the other's push is real'). Under that model the other's press never loads or moves anything but the clasped hands. The lab's contest model, the one the brief itself uses for the shoving match, treats each push as acting on the other and sends only its own push back to the source. In that model, if the pad doesn't carry the other's real press, nothing does, and momentum vanishes in a stalemate. So the README's argument holds within the model the lab uses. Q15 makes the shoving match follow 'the arm-wrestle rule'. If the duo's reading A were applied there, equal pushers would deadlock with nothing loading their feet, contradicting the brief's own shoving-match row ('two equal pushers both get shoved apart'). B is the consistent reading of both. B also does keep the own push backs in the ledger: they go to the shared source as +P·t and −P·t, which cancel, so no shown result differs. That is not 'absorbs nothing' in any visible sense. The consequences the duo lists (the table breaks at 6.1 t; standing, both pushed off their feet) are stated in 'What moved' and decision 10, where the owner will see them. At most the engine comment's 'physically incoherent' could say 'incoherent with the lab's contest rule (the shoving match)', but that is wording, not a defect.

With ownRecoil false: 'stalemate', tableBreaks true, by 'push', contact 17652 N. The table breaks either way, as decision 10 says ('both presses past what the table carries break it, as before'). P.pushMatch(Rex, Ollie) at the default dial gives 'bothShoved', 26.6 m/s each: B's rule, which the brief chose for the shoving match. README line 191 lists 'arm-wrestling reading B (decision 10)' for the owner to confirm. Decision 10's text gives the reason and the consequence ('Under A the table would never break with the power on (0 of 2,160 runs)').

findings.outcome: Refuted by the skeptic: decision 10 is a recorded choice with a sound reason, flagged for the owner. No change; reading B stays.
